questions.q: Identify the collective protagonist in "A Roadside Stand" and quote one phrase from stanza 1 that establishes their economic activity.
questions.a: The protagonist is the rural collective who run the roadside stand; the phrase "the little old house was out with a little new shed / In front at the edge of the road where the traffic sped" (stanza 1) establishes their attempt to sell produce. A wrong answer naming a single individual (e.g., "the farmer") reveals the student misses Frost's deliberate collectivisation — the stand represents a class, not a person.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the protagonist's "childish longing" (stanza 3) is not actually childish, using evidence from the poem.
questions.a: The longing is called "childish" by the indifferent city voice, but the protagonist's desire for "city money" to access "the movies" and "the requisite lift of spirit" reflects a legitimate aspiration for economic participation and cultural inclusion denied by systemic neglect. A wrong answer agreeing it is childish shows the student adopts the poem's ironic city perspective instead of analysing the dramatic irony Frost creates.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "silent characterisation" to analyse how Frost reveals the protagonist's dignity in stanza 2 without giving them a single spoken line.
questions.a: Frost uses the stand's careful construction ("artlessly painted," "wild berries in wooden quarts") and the owners' patient waiting ("waiting all day... for the squeal of brakes") to show pride in work and hope without dialogue. A wrong answer claiming "the poem doesn't show their feelings" reveals inability to read character through setting and action — a core poetry skill.

questions.q: Analyse the contrast between the protagonist's "requisite lift of spirit" (stanza 3) and the "polished traffic's" "mind ahead" (stanza 1) to explain how Frost structures class conflict through character opposition.
questions.a: The protagonist's "lift of spirit" is an active, communal hope for upward mobility, while the traffic's "mind ahead" is a selfish, individualistic forward motion that literally and metaphorically bypasses the rural poor; Frost juxtaposes collective aspiration against atomic indifference. A wrong answer describing only physical speed vs. stillness misses the psychological dimension Frost builds through diction ("polished" vs. "artlessly").

questions.q: Evaluate whether the poem's ending ("I can't help owning the great relief it would be / To put these people at one stroke out of their pain") reflects the speaker's empathy or complicity with the state violence hinted at in "greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey."
questions.a: The speaker's "relief" is a moment of exhausted empathy that dangerously flirts with the same eliminationist logic as the "greedy good-doers" — Frost implicates the reader in the temptation to erase suffering by erasing the sufferer. A wrong answer calling it "pure sympathy" ignores the ironic echo of "beneficent beasts of prey" and fails to see the speaker as morally compromised.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in Frost's voice from the perspective of the roadside stand owners responding to the "greedy good-doers" who promise "to buy their farms and move them to the village."
questions.a: A strong stanza mirrors Frost's plain diction and iambic rhythm, e.g.: "They speak of villages with paved streets, / Of schools and hospitals and seats. / But when the bulldozer drinks the mud, / We'll still be standing in the wood." A weak answer uses modern slang or explicit anger, missing Frost's restraint — the protagonist's power lies in quiet endurance, not protest.
